 Miami Heat News Davion Mitchell says Heat aren’t helping enough on defense ahead of opener
 Last updated: October 19, 2026 8:05 pm 
 Heat Nation staff 
 Share 
 7 Min Read 
 IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect 
 Davion Mitchell sees a problem with the Miami Heat’s defense that individual talent alone cannot solve: Players are trusting a teammate to handle his assignment without giving him enough help.
 Ahead of Wednesday’s season opener against the Minnesota Timberwolves, Mitchell offered a specific explanation for why Miami’s collection of capable defenders still needs work as a unit.
 The issue, in his telling, is how the other players respond while a teammate is defending the ball.
 “I feel like in practice we’re doing a really good job, but we got to put it together in the game,” Mitchell said. “We’re all really good individual defenders. And I think that sometimes we get lost in how good the defender is. So we kind of don’t help as much. We think he got it. But it’s a team game for a reason.”
 In his Monday interview posted by the Heat , Mitchell described a gap between the team’s work in practice and its execution against opponents. He also identified collective rebounding as part of the job.
 His explanation gives Miami something more specific to address than simply demanding better defense.
 A strong matchup at the point of attack still requires the other four players to stay involved, especially when the opponent can turn one defensive mistake into an advantage elsewhere.
 Mitchell soon connected that concern to Anthony Edwards. He credited Edwards’ expanding offensive skill set, including his ability to score from different areas and create for teammates, and said containing him requires a coordinated effort.
 Bam Adebayo sets a high target while acknowledging unfinished chemistry
 Bam Adebayo’s assessment of his partnership with Giannis Antetokounmpo helps explain why Miami’s expectations and its current level of execution can be different.
 Asked Sunday whether the two would begin the season fully synchronized, Adebayo said their adjustment would continue once the regular season started .
 He emphasized their willingness to improve together rather than presenting the pairing as a completed project.
 “No, not regular season sync,” Adebayo said.
 That distinction matters when evaluating the opening game. Miami can expect better decisions and more consistent support without treating one night’s performance as a final judgment on the frontcourt pairing.
 Learning a teammate’s tendencies and executing against another team’s offense are related tasks, but they are not interchangeable.
 In that same interview, Adebayo connected the players’ individual defensive ambitions to the team’s results.
 His position was that Miami needed to pursue the league’s best defense through participation across the roster, rather than leaving that responsibility to a few prominent players.
 He also welcomed the increased expectations surrounding the team, describing them as a positive for the locker room.
 The confidence was accompanied by a measured approach to the schedule: deal with the opener first and build from there.
 Giannis previously identified communication and rebounding as priorities
 The defensive work did not begin with Mitchell’s comments Monday. In an interview, Antetokounmpo identified communication, rebounding and greater physicality near the basket as areas that needed improvement.
 He extended that responsibility to whichever frontcourt combination was playing. His point was about the team’s interior work across different groups, not merely what he and Adebayo could accomplish together.
 Antetokounmpo also explained how securing the ball connects to Miami’s preferred offensive pace.
 He wanted teammates to trust the player collecting the rebound and move upcourt instead of gathering around to determine who would bring the ball forward.
 That creates a practical link between the two ends. A successful defensive possession has to finish with control of the ball before Miami can consistently benefit from playing quickly.
 For a team trying to run, rebounding is part of creating its next scoring opportunity.
 Antetokounmpo praised Adebayo’s communication during their early games together, describing his efforts to help him settle into the new setting.
 He nevertheless made clear that familiarity with teammates and different combinations would require additional repetitions.
 Those earlier comments provide context for Monday’s admission without establishing that every preseason problem remains unchanged.
 Communication, help and rebounding are separate responsibilities that have to work together; improvement in one does not automatically resolve the others.
 Minnesota will test more than Miami’s individual matchups
 Erik Spoelstra’s assessment of the Timberwolves explains why Mitchell’s concern has immediate relevance.
 In his Sunday media availability , Spoelstra described how LaMelo Ball’s passing can produce opportunities before the defense is set and allow Edwards to spend more time away from the ball.
 He highlighted Ball’s ability to find teammates near the rim as another part of the challenge.
 Adebayo offered a similar assessment in his Sunday interview, explaining that Edwards can concentrate more on attacking from favorable positions when someone else handles the initial playmaking.
 For Miami, that means the assignment extends beyond winning a stationary one-on-one matchup.
 Defenders must recognize where the next threat is developing, including when Edwards is receiving the ball rather than initiating the possession himself.
 Spoelstra also described Minnesota as an athletic team with speed and the ability to apply perimeter pressure.
 That adds another demand: Miami needs to organize its defense while managing an opponent that can make the game move quickly at both ends.
 There are still personnel decisions around that work. Everyone on Miami’s roster participated in practice, including Pelle Larsson and Dru Smith, who had missed preseason time.
 Spoelstra described their progress positively without confirming their availability for the opener.
 Spoelstra expects the rotation to remain adjustable during the season. Establishing reliable defensive habits across those combinations is therefore part of the task, alongside identifying which players will share the floor.
 Wednesday offers the first regular-season test of that work.
 Mitchell has identified a clear place to start: The Heat need their defenders to support one another throughout the possession, even when they trust the player handling the toughest individual assignment.
